hypotheses.title: SCReAM bottleneck-phase sender rate is lower than GCC's on capacity-step networks
hypotheses.claim: SCReAM's bottleneck-phase sender rate is lower than GCC's on capacity-step networks.
hypotheses.source: Zhang 2019 SIMUtools plus project fast-transition extension
hypotheses.prediction: On capacity-step networks, SCReAM's bottleneck-phase encoder-rate utilization should be lower than GCC's by at least 5 percentage points, and GCC's bottleneck-phase encoder-rate variability should be at least 20% higher.
hypotheses.verdict_rule: Supported when both utilization and variability thresholds hold; refuted when they do not. Current interpretation is regime-dependent across slow-changing and fast-changing capacity-step networks.

established_claims: SCReAM/GCC ranking depends on the transition time scale of the capacity-step network.
Sender-side utilization and receiver-side delivered frames answer different questions.
limits: The result is not a general claim that either algorithm is globally better.

hypotheses.title: GCC stays ahead across latency-deadline and retransmission settings
hypotheses.claim: On the fluctuating network, GCC delivers more viewer frames than SCReAM across latency-deadline and retransmission settings.
hypotheses.prediction: On the fluctuating 5 Mbps/300 kbps capacity-step network, GCC should deliver more median viewer frames than SCReAM in every crossed cell of retransmission on/off and latency budget 0/50/100 ms.
hypotheses.verdict_rule: Supported if all six deadline/retransmission cells show GCC ahead of SCReAM by at least 30 median viewer frames; inconclusive if only some cells meet the margin; refuted if the margin disappears.

experiments.name: retransmission-deadline-fluc
experiments.role: fluctuating-network CC deadline and retransmission comparison

established_claims: GCC delivers more median viewer frames than SCReAM in every tested deadline/retransmission cell on the fluctuating network.
Neither deadline enforcement nor retransmission changes the SCReAM-vs-GCC ranking in this experiment.
limits: This is a fluctuating-network ranking result, not a general claim about NACK or latency budgets on every network.

hypotheses.title: Media workload calibration gates realistic 5G trace comparisons
hypotheses.claim: Media workload calibration gates realistic 5G trace comparisons.
hypotheses.source: Project-internal validity check for realistic-trace SCReAM/GCC experiments
hypotheses.prediction: The current ball-720p30-30s VP8 workload is not valid for comparing SCReAM and GCC on the translated 5G traces because observed camera wire bitrate is far below trace capacity. A workload is considered under-driving when each translated 5G trace has at least 10x median capacity headroom over observed camera wire bitrate and fewer than 15% of 100 ms bins below 1 Mbit/s.
hypotheses.verdict_rule: Supported if all tested realistic traces meet the under-driving rule; inconclusive if only some do; refuted if none do; untested if required records are absent.

environment.transport: Tailscale hostnames from hosts.yaml for media/control addressing
environment.sync_scope: allowlisted project files needed to run the selected experiment

established_claims: The current ball-720p30-30s VP8 workload emits roughly 220-230 kbit/s, far below the typical capacity of the translated 5G traces.
The previous realistic-trace SCReAM/GCC comparisons should not be interpreted as meaningful algorithm comparisons.
A future realistic-trace comparison must first pass this calibration gate with a high-quality or high-bitrate workload whose observed wire bitrate actually stresses the trace.
limits: This validates that the old workload is too light; it does not yet test a replacement high-quality workload.
Brief low-capacity fades still exist in the handover-like traces; the claim is about typical headroom across the full replay.

hypotheses.title: SCReAM preserves more decodable video than GCC on calibrated stressed realistic 5G traces
hypotheses.claim: SCReAM preserves more decodable video than GCC on calibrated stressed realistic 5G traces.
hypotheses.prediction: On fixed translated 5G Mahimahi traces scaled to 33% capacity, a calibrated high-entropy 384x216x30 VP8 workload should show where the controller matters. CQI is expected to act as a high-capacity control where both controllers deliver nearly all frames. On the stressed HO and RB traces, SCReAM should deliver more viewer-depayloaded frames than GCC while using no more than 85% of GCC's camera egress bitrate and reaching a similar viewer-side ingress bitrate.
hypotheses.verdict_rule: Supported if all experiment runs pass, both stressed traces show SCReAM/GCC viewer-frame ratio >=1.25, both stressed traces show camera egress mean bitrate <=85% of GCC, viewer-side mean wire bitrate is within 10% of GCC on stressed traces, and at least one stressed trace shows >=2x viewer-frame ratio. Refuted if completed records fail those thresholds; untested if required records or summaries are missing.

experiments.name: scream-vs-gcc-mahimahi-5g-cqi-x0p33-snow-384x216
experiments.role: fixed realistic CQI-like high-capacity control trace

conclusions.mechanism_claim: SCReAM wins on the stressed HO/RB traces because its post-payload RTP pacing turns congestion-control decisions into lower camera egress, while GCC lowers its estimator target but this pipeline still emits multi-Mbit/s RTP that the trace cannot carry, leaving fewer complete frames decodable at the viewer.
supporting_subclaims: Within each trace pair, the trace, video, codec, bitrate bounds, recovery settings, sink, workers, and run length are fixed; only congestion_control.algorithm varies.
CQI is the high-capacity control and both controllers deliver nearly all frames, so the advantage appears only when HO/RB capacity actually stresses the stream.
On HO, SCReAM delivers 2.74x GCC's viewer frames; on RB, it delivers 1.39x GCC's viewer frames.
The advantage is not from sending more traffic; SCReAM uses 0.72x GCC's camera egress on HO and 0.64x on RB.
GCC's target falls on the stressed traces, but its measured camera egress remains about 2.35 Mbit/s on HO and 2.32 Mbit/s on RB.
established_claims: On the calibrated fixed CQI x0.33 trace, both controllers delivered nearly all frames, so this trace is a high-capacity control rather than evidence of a SCReAM advantage.
On the calibrated fixed HO x0.33 trace, SCReAM delivered roughly 2.7x as many viewer-depayloaded frames as GCC while producing lower camera egress.
On the calibrated fixed RB x0.33 trace, SCReAM delivered about 1.4x as many viewer-depayloaded frames as GCC while producing lower camera egress.
GCC's estimator target does drop on the stressed traces, but in this pipeline that target is not equivalent to lower post-encoder RTP egress.

established_claims.The result is meaningful because the wor: observed media bitrate is in the same range as the scaled trace capacities.

limits: This is a fixed-trace, fixed-workload result; CQI shows that SCReAM does not produce a visible frame-delivery advantage when the trace has enough capacity for both controllers.
The current latency metric still has clock-skew artifacts; H4's primary claim is decodable frame delivery and camera egress.

hypotheses.title: Our SCReAM adapts to changing bandwidth better than UMN's reimplementation — because UMN's controller can't drive its encoder, not because of the algorithm
hypotheses.claim: When the available bandwidth keeps changing, our SCReAM raises and lowers its sending rate to match what the link can carry, so it uses most of the available bandwidth. UMN's reimplementation instead holds a roughly constant sending rate, so it leaves most of a fast link unused. The reason is what we call a controller-to-encoder gap: the congestion controller (the part that decides how fast to send) picks a sending rate, but that decision is never applied to the video encoder, so the encoder keeps producing video at roughly the same rate no matter what. This is a plumbing problem inside UMN's implementation — not a flaw in the SCReAM algorithm itself, and not a matter of how often its control loop runs. (A Glossary at the end defines any remaining term.)
hypotheses.source: Project-internal cross-implementation comparison against UMN Teleop-Gopher-streamer (scream-integration branch 502533c)
hypotheses.prediction: Both stacks stream the same 60 s clip on one machine over loopback (sender and receiver are two processes on the same host). The network is squeezed the same way for both: a Linux traffic shaper on the loopback interface replays recorded 5G bandwidth patterns — a sudden handover drop (HO), bumpy tower-sharing (RB), and smooth signal drift (CQI) — each scaled to 1/3 capacity so the link is tight. Both get the same bitrate limits, and UMN's network_time_sync flag is on so its delay signal (the cue SCReAM uses to sense a building queue, and back off) actually works. We expect: our SCReAM's sending rate rises and falls with the available bandwidth, so it uses most of what the link offers — high "utilization", the share of available bandwidth actually used — while UMN's stays near a constant rate across the three traces, whose capacities differ about 2.5x. We also expect the gap to remain when UMN's control loop is sped up (re-checking every 50 ms instead of 200 ms) and made to ramp up faster — which would rule out loop timing as the cause — and to line up with the controller-to-encoder gap measured directly: the rate actually sent exceeds the rate the controller asked for, in most decisions.
hypotheses.verdict_rule: Supported when (a) on the high-capacity CQI trace our utilization is at least 2x UMN's; (b) UMN's mean sent rate barely changes across the three traces (spread <= 15%), showing it does not track capacity; (c) speeding up UMN's loop to 50 ms and raising its ramp gain do not raise its CQI utilization (timing ruled out); and (d) the diagnostic shows the actual sent rate exceeding the controller's commanded target by more than 1.3x in most decisions. Refuted if the utilization gap closes once the delay signal is on, or if faster timing recovers utilization. Untested if the comparison metrics are missing.

environment.topology: single host, loopback (127.0.0.1) — sender and receiver are two processes on the same machine
environment.shaper: tc qdisc on the loopback interface (fixed 20 ms delay + a bandwidth cap that changes every 100 ms to follow the 5G trace)
environment.our_stack: GStreamer 1.24, config 90 (SCReAM via the gstscream plugin), streaming realmotion.avi
environment.workload: realmotion.avi — a 1280x1024 Motion-JPEG clip at 10 frames/sec, 60 s long
environment.note: This is a cross-implementation comparison run by a dedicated harness (tools/comparison_sweep.sh, umn_scream_rerun.sh, umn_ladder.sh, tc_lo_driver.py), not by experiment.py, so this hypothesis has no internal experiment.py records. The evidence is the tables and figures below; the raw per-run numbers are in analysis/umn-comparison/metrics.csv.

conclusions.mechanism_claim: With both implementations configured fairly, our SCReAM changes its sending rate to track the available bandwidth, while UMN's holds a near-constant rate. The cause is a controller-to-encoder gap: UMN's controller decides on a rate, but that decision is not applied to the encoder, so the encoder keeps producing video at roughly the same rate regardless. This is not explained by the SCReAM algorithm or by how often the control loop runs.
supporting_subclaims: On the high-capacity CQI trace, our SCReAM uses about 63% of the available bandwidth; UMN's uses about 22%.
UMN's sending rate stays near 776-780 kbps on all three traces, even though their capacities differ about 2.5x — so it is not following the link.
Speeding up UMN's control loop (200 ms to 50 ms) and making it ramp faster did not raise its utilization — so loop timing is not the cause.

The controller-to-encoder gap is measured directly - the actual sent rate exceeded the controller's commanded rate by more than 1.3x in about 89% of decisions; UMN's packet-loss congestion signal also never fired.
established_claims: Utilization (the share of available bandwidth actually used) on the high-capacity CQI trace: ours ~63%, UMN ~22%.
UMN's SCReAM sends a near-constant ~776-782 kbps across the HO, RB, and CQI traces, whose capacities differ about 2.5x; it does not raise its rate when more bandwidth is available.
The shortfall is a controller-to-encoder gap (the controller's chosen rate is not applied to the encoder), not the SCReAM algorithm or its loop timing.

Pinpointed in code: in encoder.py the encode loop applies the controller's rate by writing codec.bit_rate on an already-running software encoder, which libav ignores (a software encoder's bitrate is fixed when it opens). Only a full encoder reopen changes the rate, and the libvpx path never triggers that reopen — so the rate is set once at startup. This is a wiring problem in the implementation, not the SCReAM algorithm.

Architecture difference: UMN runs the controller as a separate thread that leaves a per-frame "budget" the encode loop must apply by hand, per codec; our SCReAM is a built-in pipeline element whose rate the media framework applies to the encoder automatically. The reference + framework-integrated design avoids this class of bug.

Algorithm fidelity (from source-code review, NOT measured in this experiment — the wiring gap masked it): the reference SCReAM is a queue-delay-gradient controller with a congestion window, bytes-in-flight limiting, and adaptive step sizes; UMN's is a fixed-gain multiply-up (x1.05) / multiply-down (x0.8) loop on binary signals with no memory. So the maturity case has two independent legs — a simpler control law (code-level) and an open control loop on the software path (measured). See the algorithm-comparison table.

An earlier version of this comparison showed UMN overshooting the link badly; that was our configuration mistake (network_time_sync was off, which disables UMN's delay signal). With it on, UMN no longer overshoots — confirming that result was an artifact, not a property of UMN's controller.
UMN's delay congestion signal works once network_time_sync is on; its packet-loss signal never fires in these runs.
limits: Single-host loopback reproduces the bandwidth and delay faithfully but not real 5G radio effects (interference, scheduling, retransmission at the radio layer).

We measured network behavior (utilization, overshoot, sent rate), not delivered picture quality (PSNR/SSIM). "Uses the link better" is a statement about bandwidth use, not yet a measured video-quality difference.
UMN's controller is an early reimplementation (its own code marks receiver feedback as a future phase). This is a snapshot of branch 502533c, not a statement about the SCReAM algorithm in general.

Encode path (corrected): only UMN's VAAPI path reopens the encoder when the bitrate changes. NVENC — which UMN actually deploys — takes the SAME PyAV path as the libvpx encoder we tested: it applies the controller's rate with a live codec.bit_rate write and never reopens (NVENC uses in-band keyframes). libav fixes an encoder's bitrate when it opens and ignores later writes, so the controller-to-encoder gap almost certainly affects UMN's deployed NVENC path too — not just the software path. (An earlier draft wrongly implied the hardware path escapes the gap; that described VAAPI, which UMN does not deploy.)

Open question / verify next: NVENC behavior here is inferred from the code (PyAV path + libav's open-time bitrate), not measured — there is no NVIDIA GPU on the bench. Confirming it needs an NVENC run on real hardware under the same traces.
Open question / verify next: we measured network behavior (utilization), not delivered video quality. The honest quality metric is PSNR/SSIM of the received video vs the source, on both stacks.
